name: Question 15
problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\theta  & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}\theta =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}-0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}+(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Evaluate the integral of the function f(x,y)=xarcsin⁡y along the polar curve r=1 for 0≤θ≤π3.

a
3π+12
b
3π−32
c
3−12
d
3π−36
e
3π6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos⁡θ and y=sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π3.

Now, since f(x,y)=xarcsin⁡y, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos⁡θarcsin⁡(sin⁡θ)=θcos⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(1)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=12+02=1.

We can now write the integral as

∫Cxarcsin⁡yds=∫0π/3f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/3θcos⁡θ⋅1⋅dθ=∫0π/3θcos⁡θdθ.

Let's use integration by parts. We denote u=θ⟹u′=1,v′=cos⁡θ⟹v=∫v′dθ=∫cos⁡θdθ=sin⁡θ.

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain

∫0π/3θcos⁡θdθ=θsin⁡θ|0π/3−∫0π/3sin⁡θdθ=(3π6−0)+cos⁡θ|0π/3=3π6+(12−1)=3π−36.
